name: Adam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go for it. I like talking about this, I've been reading about farm robots for years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent about 120 hectares on a five-year tenancy, with 500 ewes and some wheat and oilseed rape, and I run a contracting business on the side, baling, hedge cutting and drilling for other farms. Most mornings I check the sheep on the quad, then I'm out with the tractor on someone else's job by nine. I love being my own boss; the paperwork and chasing people to pay invoices is what wears me down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, rent a cottage at the bottom of the valley, play rugby on Saturdays and go to church most Sundays. My money's in my machinery, which I own outright, and about eight months of cash. I use AI every day for quotes, booking jobs, the weather and selling grain at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, like a GPS or a good dog. AI already writes my contracting quotes and plans my baling rounds, and I'd keep using it the way I use a good dog. I'd say that to the lads at rugby, who mostly don't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is fine for me. The contracting business is growing, the sheep pay, I own my kit. My biggest worry is the tenancy coming up in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep growing the contracting, maybe buy a second baler next spring. Keep using AI for quotes and invoices. Keep my cash topped up for when the tenancy comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the tenancy.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's from an estate, and the land agent can put the rent up or let it to someone bigger. I'd want enough cash to bid for it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a second baler cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty thousand second-hand. It'd pay for itself in three seasons if I keep the customers I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers who adapt will do well and those who don't will struggle. That's how markets work. Most farmers round here hate paperwork more than mud, so I'd sell them a contracting service that does both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I'm already using AI, so I'm ahead of most. The robots coming slowly gives me time to work out which ones are worth buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering farms a package: I do the field work and the AI handles their records and subsidy forms. I'd try a weeding robot on hire on my own rape crop next year. And I'd keep an eye out for small farms whose owners are retiring, for more tenancy land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would buy that package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older farmers mostly, like Mr Price up the valley, who's seventy and still does his forms by hand. He'd pay to never see a form again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone around you going to lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm secretaries who go round doing paperwork. I'd feel bad, but I'm not going to not do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots by 2031. That's tight even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge opportunity and people should get ready. I'd say government shouldn't block it, but it should help with apprenticeships. I'd say families need to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's a race. If the big machinery dealers rent out robots by 2031, my contracting business is finished unless I get there first. My sheep might be fine longer, but the tenancy rent could go up as land gets more valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'd sell my old tractors while they're still worth something and buy the first robots I can get finance on. I'd borrow against the business if I had to. And I'd ask the estate for a longer tenancy now, before everything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious, because I might lose the race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lose the race?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies with more money. If John Deere rents a robot for less than my diesel costs, I can't compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on debt in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd borrow maybe a hundred thousand. Strong cushion or not, that's a big bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real head start for someone ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time for young farmers who plan. I'd say that at the young farmers' club and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out ahead. Five years is long enough for me to be the man with the robots that every small farm round here rings in the spring. The dealers will go for big farms first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start using robots on my own land, on hire, to learn them. By 2031 I'd buy two or three and offer robot contracting to the valley. I'd still keep the sheep, because they're my steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots aren't reliable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have a tractor in the shed. I'm not selling everything until they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever stop farming yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd be running the business more, but I'd still check my ewes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd say young people should learn the machines and the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is ideal. Ten years is time to build a proper business, marry a good woman and pay off the machines before the robots arrive. I'd be about forty when they come, with a business and hopefully a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the contracting the normal way. I'd look for a bigger tenancy or even buy a bit of land around 2030. And I'd keep using AI to run the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is the version I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said marry a good woman. Is that on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, yeah. My mum asks every Sunday. Ten years gives me time to sort that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the tenancy. Always the tenancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Big dealers could beat me before I'm ready. Whoever owns the machines in this valley will do fine, and I intend to be the one who owns them. What would help is a longer tenancy and apprenticeships on farm robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about tenancies. Half the young farmers I know rent, and the landlords will do well whatever the robots do.

He's single, owns his **machinery** outright and has eight months of cash.
He uses AI **every day** and wants to be the valley's robot contractor.
He's **calm** in most pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028, racing big dealers.
His lasting worry is his **estate tenancy**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because big dealers could beat him before he's ready.
